# The why of databases


## Numbers every programmer should know

| Task                                | Timing (ns)       | Timing (μs)       |
|-------------------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| L1 cache reference                  | 0.5               | 0.0005            |
| L2 cache reference                  | 7                 | 0.007             |
| Main memory reference               | 100               | 0.1               |
| Random seek SSD                     | 150,000           | 150               |
| Read 1 MB sequentially from memory  | 250,000           | 250               |
| Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD     | 1,000,000         | 1,000             |
| Disk seek                           | 10,000,000        | 10,000            |  
| Read 1 MB sequentially from disk    | 20,000,000        | 20,000            |
| Send packet CA->Netherlands->CA     | 150,000,000       | 150,000           |


::: {.aside}
From [jboner/latency.txt](https://gist.github.com/jboner/2841832) & [sirupsen/napkin-math](https://github.com/sirupsen/napkin-math) <br/>
Jeff Dean's original [talk](http://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en/us/people/jeff/stanford-295-talk.pdf) 
:::


## Implications for big data

Let's imagine we have a *10 GB* flat data file and that we want to select certain rows based on a particular criterion (filtering). 

This requires a sequential read across the entire data set.


| File Location    | Performance                        | Time        |
|:-----------------|:-----------------------------------|:------------|
| in memory        | $10~GB \times (250~\mu s / 1~MB)$  | 2.5 seconds |
| on disk (SSD)    | $10~GB \times (1~ms / 1~MB)$       | 10 seconds  |
| on disk (HD)     | $10~GB \times (20~ms / 1~MB)$      | 200 seconds |

<br/>

This is just for *reading* the sequential data, if we make any modifications (*writing*) or the data is fragmented things are much worse. 


## Blocks

#### Cost:
::: {.center}
 Disk << SSD <<< Memory
:::


#### Speed:
::: {.center}
Disk <<< SSD << Memory
:::

<br/>

::: {.fragment}
Disk is cheap but slow; memory is fast but limited. 

What do we do when our data doesn't fit in memory?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Create *blocks* — group related rows and read multiple rows at a time, loading only what's needed (skip what we dont want). 

Optimal block size depends on the task and the storage medium.
:::


## Linear vs Binary Search

Blocks reduce I/O, but any query still requires scanning all of them — a linear search requiring $\mathcal{O}(N)$ reads.

. . .

<br/>

We can do better if we are careful about how we structure our data, specifically sorting some (or all) of the columns.

* Sorting is expensive, $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$, but it only needs to be done once. 

* After sorting, we can use a binary search for any subsetting tasks, $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$

* In databases these "sorted" columns are referred to as *indexes*.

* Indexes require additional storage, but are usually small enough to be kept in memory even when the blocks need to stay on disk.


## So why databases?

Implementing blocks, indexes, and query optimization correctly is hard:

* The optimal strategy depends on your queries — and they change

* Data is modified (inserts, updates, deletes) — structures must stay consistent

* Multiple users may access data simultaneously — concurrency must be managed

* Failures happen — data must remain correct and recoverable

::: {.fragment}
A database management system (DBMS) handles all of this for you, plus provides a standard query language (SQL) to express what you want, not how to get it.
:::


# Flights

## The data

`nycflights13`: 336,776 flights departing NYC in 2013.

```{r}
nycflights13::flights |>
  select(month, day, origin, dest, carrier, dep_delay) |>
  glimpse()
```

How did October departure delays differ across airlines and airports?

`dep_delay` is in minutes; negative values indicate early departures.

## October departure delays

```{r}
nycflights13::flights |>
  filter(month == 10, !is.na(dep_delay)) |>
  group_by(origin, carrier) |>
  summarise(
    n_flights = n(),
    mean_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

## SQLite and DBI 

| Tool | Role |
|---|---|
| SQLite | Database engine, running inside our process |
| RSQLite | R driver for SQLite |
| DBI | Common interface for connections and SQL |
| dbplyr | Translates supported dplyr operations to SQL |

- **SQLite** needs no separate server. It acts as the actual storage container for your data. Unlike major databases like PostgreSQL or MySQL, SQLite stores the entire database as a single file on your local computer, (fast and easy for local projects / small applications).

- **DBI** acts as the translator or "bridge" between your programming environment (specifically R) and the database. It provides a standardized set of commands (like connecting, disconnecting, or sending raw SQL queries) so that you don't have to learn a completely new programming syntax every time you switch from SQLite to PostgreSQL


## Set up a database

```{r}
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(dplyr)
library(dbplyr)

db = dbConnect(SQLite(), "flights.sqlite")

dbWriteTable(
  db, "flights", nycflights13::flights,
  overwrite = TRUE
)
dbWriteTable(
  db, "airlines", nycflights13::airlines,
  overwrite = TRUE
)

dbListTables(db)
```

- "flights.sqlite" is the database file in the current working directory. SQLite creates it if it does not exist; otherwise, it opens the existing file.
- `overwrite = TRUE` replaces these tables when rerunning the example.

## tbl()

```{r}
flight_tbl = tbl(db, "flights")
airlines_tbl = tbl(db, "airlines")

flight_tbl |>
  select(origin, carrier, dep_delay)
```

- tbl() creates an R reference to the "flights" table in the database
- `flight_tbl` describes a database table. It is not a local copy of every row. We can send queries using `dplyr` functions.

## Filter and select

```{r}
oct_21 = flight_tbl |>
  filter(month == 10, day == 21) |>
  select(origin, dest, carrier, tailnum, dep_delay)

oct_21
```

## dplyr to SQL

```{r}
oct_21 |> show_query()
```
Read `SELECT`, `FROM`, and `WHERE` as: columns, source, and row conditions.

## dbGetQuery()

```{r}
DBI::dbGetQuery(db, "
  SELECT origin, dest, carrier, dep_delay
  FROM flights
  WHERE month = 10 AND day = 21
  LIMIT 6
")
```

## Laziness

Building a pipeline records work to do.

* `show_query()` displays SQL.
* Printing a lazy table retrieves a preview.
* `collect()` executes and brings the result into R.
* `compute()` executes and stores a result table in the database.
* `collapse()` restructures SQL without executing it.

. . .

A preview with few rows can still require substantial database work.

## Summarize October delays

```{r}
october_summary = flight_tbl |>
  filter(month == 10, !is.na(dep_delay)) |>
  group_by(origin, carrier) |>
  summarise(
    n_flights = n(),
    mean_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

october_summary
```

## Exercise: when does work happen?

For each expression, predict what happens in R and in the database.

```r
q = flight_tbl |> filter(month == 10)
show_query(q)
q
collect(q)
```

Which expression brings **all matching rows** into R?

## Collect early or late?

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Collect early**
```r
flight_tbl |>
  collect() |>
  count(origin)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Collect late**
```r
flight_tbl |>
  count(origin) |>
  collect()
```
:::
::::

Same counts. Very different amounts of data enter R.

## Result sizes

```{r}
all_flights = collect(flight_tbl)
small_result = flight_tbl |> count(origin) |> collect()

tibble(
  result = c("All flights", "Airport counts"),
  rows = c(nrow(all_flights), nrow(small_result)),
  bytes_in_R = c(as.numeric(object.size(all_flights)),
                 as.numeric(object.size(small_result)))
)
```
Object sizes describe these R results, not peak memory or database memory.

## Timing collect()

```{r}
early = function() {
  flight_tbl |> collect() |> count(origin) |> arrange(origin)
}
late = function() {
  flight_tbl |> count(origin) |> arrange(origin) |> collect()
}
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(early(), late())))
system.time(early())
system.time(late())
```

## Join airline names

```{r}
named_summary = october_summary |>
  left_join(airlines_tbl, by = "carrier") |>
  select(origin, carrier, name, n_flights, mean_delay) |>
  arrange(origin, desc(mean_delay))

named_summary
```

## Join keys

```{r}
airlines_tbl |>
  count(carrier) |>
  filter(n != 1) |>
  collect()
```
A lookup should have one row per `carrier`.

Join by meaning, not by row position.

## Joins across sources

```{r}
local_df = data.frame(origin = c("JFK", "LGA"))
```

```{r}
#| error: true
flight_tbl |> inner_join(local_df, by = "origin")
```

The local data frame and database table have different sources.

## A local lookup table

```{r}
flight_tbl |>
  inner_join(local_df, by = "origin", copy = TRUE) |>
  count(origin) |>
  collect()
```

`copy = TRUE` copies the small lookup into the database.

## EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN

```{r}
lookup_sql = "
  SELECT origin, dest, dep_delay
  FROM flights
  WHERE month = 10 AND day = 21
"
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  db, paste("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN", lookup_sql)
)
```

## CREATE INDEX

```{r}
DBI::dbExecute(db, "
  CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS flights_date_idx
  ON flights(month, day)
")
DBI::dbGetQuery(
  db, paste("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN", lookup_sql)
)
```
Compare `SCAN` with `SEARCH ... USING INDEX` in the plan.

## Ranking delays

```{r}
extreme_delays = flight_tbl |>
  filter(month == 10, !is.na(dep_delay)) |>
  group_by(origin) |>
  mutate(delay_rank = min_rank(desc(dep_delay))) |>
  filter(delay_rank <= 3) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(origin, carrier, dep_delay, delay_rank) |>
  arrange(origin, delay_rank)

extreme_delays
```

## Window functions

Window functions compute a value for each row using values from a surrounding partition.
Within a `group_by()` + `mutate()`, dplyr translates these to `SQL OVER()` clauses:

```{r}
extreme_delays |> show_query()
```
Look for `OVER` and `PARTITION BY`: calculate within each airport while retaining rows.

## An R function inside a query

```{r}
starts_with_n = function(x) grepl("^N", x)
```

```{r}
#| error: true
custom_query = oct_21 |>
  mutate(n_prefix = starts_with_n(tailnum))
custom_query |> show_query()
```

```{r}
#| error: true
oct_21 |>
  mutate(n_prefix = starts_with_n(tailnum)) |>
  collect()
```

SQLite cannot call this function from the R session.

## Collect, then use the R function

```{r}
oct_21 |>
  select(tailnum) |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(n_prefix = starts_with_n(tailnum)) |>
  head(6)
```

Filter and select in the database; apply the R-only function after collection.

## Missing values in SQL

```{r}
#| warning: true
dbplyr::translate_sql(mean(dep_delay), con = db)
```

```{r}
dbplyr::translate_sql(mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE), con = db)
```

SQL aggregates generally ignore `NULL`; local R's `mean()` defaults to `na.rm = FALSE`.

## collect()

```{r}
delay_results = named_summary |> collect()

delay_results |>
  select(origin, name, n_flights, mean_delay) |>
  head(8)
```
Now use R for plots or further analysis of the compact result.

## compute()

```{r}
cached_summary = october_summary |> compute()

cached_summary |>
  left_join(airlines_tbl, by = "carrier") |>
  collect()
```
`compute()` stores the summary in the database; it does not download it.

## Loading data larger than RAM

`copy_to(db, a_large_tibble)` requires that tibble to exist in R first.

At scale:

* Connect to an existing database, or load data in bounded batches.
* Reuse the persistent database across analyses.
* Filter and summarize before collecting.
* Consider an analytical engine such as DuckDB for scan-heavy workloads (next time)

## Exercise: a compact route summary

For October flights with observed departure delay:

1. Keep flights departing from JFK.
2. Calculate flight count and mean delay for each destination.
3. Keep destinations with at least 50 such flights.
4. Sort by decreasing mean delay and collect the result.

Before running: where should `collect()` go, and why?

## Exercise solution

```{r}
route_summary = flight_tbl |>
  filter(month == 10, origin == "JFK", !is.na(dep_delay)) |>
  group_by(dest) |>
  summarise(
    n_flights = n(),
    mean_delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n_flights >= 50) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_delay), dest) |>
  collect()
head(route_summary)
```

## dbDisconnect()

```{r}
DBI::dbDisconnect(db)
```

- closes the connection to the database
- deletes temporary tables (such as those created by default result of compute)
  - persistence with argument `temporary = FALSE`
- collected results remain available in R after connection closes
